title: Female External Genitalia and Sexuality Terms
body:
## What it is
The vulva is the collective name for the female external genitalia. Before the anatomy, three terms are kept apart: **sexuality** is the whole mix of feelings, attitudes, preferences and behaviors tied to being sexual; **gender** is the inner sense of being feminine or masculine; **sex** is biologic male or female status.

## Must-know structures
- **Mons pubis (mons veneris):** fat pad over the symphysis pubis, hair-covered after puberty.
- **Labia majora:** two large fatty folds that protect the urethral and vaginal openings.
- **Labia minora:** two hairless folds inside the majora.
- **Clitoris:** small erectile organ with many nerve endings; the site of sexual arousal.
- **Fourchette:** where the labia join at the back; a common site of episiotomy cuts and tears.
- **Vestibule:** almond-shaped area holding the urinary meatus, Skene's glands, the hymen, the vaginal opening and Bartholin's glands.
- **Skene's (paraurethral) glands:** a little mucus for lubrication.
- **Bartholin's (paravaginal) glands:** alkaline secretion that neutralizes vaginal acidity, helping sperm survive.
- **Hymen:** thin membrane partly covering the vaginal opening.
- **Perineum:** the muscular area between the vagina and anus.

## How the exam asks about it
Identify a structure from its function (episiotomy site = fourchette/perineum; alkaline secretion = Bartholin's). Questions on episiotomy care and perineal tears come back in [[Fourth Stage of Labor and Postpartum Checks]] and [[Postpartum Infection and Endometritis]].

## Related topics
[[Female Internal Genitalia: Vagina, Uterus and Decidua]], [[Male Reproductive Anatomy]]

title: Female Internal Genitalia: Vagina, Uterus and Decidua
body:
## Vagina
A stretchy canal that serves as the passage for menstrual flow and the baby. The anterior wall is about 6-7 cm and the posterior wall 8-9 cm. Rugae (thick folds) let it stretch without tearing during birth.

## Uterus
A hollow, pear-shaped muscular organ that houses and feeds the fetus. Non-pregnant it is about 5-7 cm long, 5 cm wide, 2.5 cm thick and weighs about 60 g; in pregnancy it becomes ovoid and weighs about 1000 g.

Parts:
- **Fundus:** top part, palpated through the abdomen to follow uterine growth.
- **Corpus (body):** expands to hold the growing fetus.
- **Isthmus:** short segment between body and cervix; the part usually cut in a cesarean birth.
- **Cervix:** lowest part, about half above and half inside the vagina.

Layers, inside to outside:
- **Endometrium:** inner lining (basal and glandular layers); what is shed in menstruation.
- **Myometrium:** muscle layer; it contracts in labor and also closes off the tubal junctions to stop menstrual blood backing up into the tubes.
- **Perimetrium:** outer layer giving strength and support.

## Decidua
"Decidua" means falling off. In pregnancy the endometrium becomes the decidua:
- **Basalis:** under the embryo (becomes the maternal side of the placenta).
- **Capsularis:** stretches over the embryo surface.
- **Vera:** the rest of the lining.

## How the exam asks about it
Fundal height as the way to track growth ([[Fundic Height Landmarks in Pregnancy]]), and the isthmus as the cesarean incision site.

## Related topics
[[Female External Genitalia and Sexuality Terms]], [[Ovaries and Fallopian Tubes]], [[Phases of the Menstrual Cycle]]

title: Ovaries and Fallopian Tubes
body:
## Ovaries
Almond-shaped, grayish-white female gonads (about 4 cm long). They **produce, mature and release ova** and make **estrogen and progesterone**, which start and regulate the menstrual cycle ([[Hormonal Control of the Menstrual Cycle]]).

## Fallopian tubes
About 10 cm long. They carry the ovum to the uterus and are where sperm meet the ovum (fertilization). Segments, from ovary to uterus:
- **Infundibulum:** funnel-shaped, about 2 cm, with finger-like fimbriae that sweep the ovum in.
- **Ampulla:** the longest segment; the usual site of fertilization **and the most common site of ectopic pregnancy**.
- **Isthmus:** the narrow part cut or sealed in tubal ligation (permanent sterilization).
- **Interstitial portion:** inside the uterine wall; the **most dangerous** ectopic site because rupture is worst here.

## Why it matters
Tube anatomy explains why an implanted embryo in the tube can rupture and bleed into the abdomen ([[Ectopic Pregnancy]]). Ligation at the isthmus ties into family planning ([[Reproductive Health and Family Planning]]).

## Related topics
[[Female Internal Genitalia: Vagina, Uterus and Decidua]], [[Ectopic Pregnancy]]

title: Male Reproductive Anatomy
body:
## External structures
- **Penis:** organ for urination and intercourse. Two corpora cavernosa (side columns of erectile tissue) and one corpus spongiosum on the underside.
- **Scrotum:** pouch holding the testes; it acts as a temperature regulator for them.
- **Testes:** two ovoid glands, 2-3 cm wide, sitting in the scrotum.

## Internal structures in the order sperm travel
- **Epididymis:** collects sperm from the testis and is where they mature.
- **Vas deferens:** carries sperm up through the inguinal canal into the abdomen.
- **Seminal vesicle:** adds the thick part of the semen (fructose, protein, prostaglandin).
- **Ejaculatory duct:** joins the seminal vesicle to the urethra.
- **Prostate gland:** alkaline fluid that protects sperm and reduces vaginal acidity.
- **Cowper's (bulbourethral) gland:** lubricating fluid into the urethra.
- **Urethra:** shared passage for urine and semen.

## How the exam asks about it
Match structure to function (fructose = seminal vesicle; sperm maturation = epididymis). Useful for family planning teaching such as vasectomy ([[Reproductive Health and Family Planning]]).

## Related topics
[[Female External Genitalia and Sexuality Terms]], [[Hormonal Control of the Menstrual Cycle]]

title: Hormonal Control of the Menstrual Cycle
body:
## Normal values from the handout
- Average cycle 28 days (range 23-35).
- Flow lasts about 4-6 days normally (1-9 counts as abnormal in the handout).
- Normal blood loss about 30-80 mL (roughly a quarter cup).

## The four-organ chain
1. **Hypothalamus** releases GnRH.
2. **Anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis)** is stimulated to release the gonadotropins.
3. **Ovaries** respond by maturing a follicle, ovulating, and making estrogen and progesterone.
4. **Uterus** builds its lining (stratum functionalis) for a possible pregnancy and sheds it if none happens.

## The two gonadotropins
- **FSH:** active early in the cycle; matures the primordial follicle.
- **LH:** most active at mid-cycle; the LH surge triggers ovulation.

## How the exam asks about it
Which hormone triggers ovulation (LH surge), which organ is the "master" (hypothalamus), and what the lining does when no pregnancy happens. The phases are detailed in [[Phases of the Menstrual Cycle]].

## Memory aid
"FSH = follicle first; LH = let go (ovulate)". Made up, not from the handout.

## Related topics
[[Phases of the Menstrual Cycle]], [[Ovaries and Fallopian Tubes]]

title: Phases of the Menstrual Cycle
body:
## Proliferative (follicular/estrogenic/post-menstrual) phase
- First phase, **length varies** (about 6-14 days in the handout).
- Just after flow the lining is very thin. Rising **estrogen** makes it grow, thickening it many-fold (about 1 mm to 8 mm).
- One follicle matures per cycle: the **Graafian follicle**, the most mature, full of estrogen-rich fluid with an ovum ready to leave.
- Peak estrogen triggers the **LH surge**, and the ovum is released: **ovulation**.

## Luteal (secretory/progestational/premenstrual) phase
- Second phase, **always about 14 days** (constant).
- The empty follicle becomes the **corpus luteum**, which makes **progesterone**.
- Progesterone maintains and organizes the lining; the glands become twisted (corkscrew) and secretory. Note: the handout also says LH peaks here, which conflicts with LH peaking at ovulation; see the check section.

## Ischemic phase
If there is no fertilization, the corpus luteum regresses after about 8-10 days. Estrogen and progesterone fall, capillaries rupture, and the lining begins to slough.

## Menstrual phase
Estrogen and progesterone are lowest; menstrual flow passes.

## Clinical tie-in
Depo-Provera (a progesterone preparation) is used for dysfunctional uterine bleeding.

## How the exam asks about it
Which phase is variable (proliferative) versus constant (luteal), and what hormone dominates each. A pregnancy test or a missed period is the reference point used in [[Signs of Pregnancy: Presumptive, Probable and Positive]].

## Check against your textbook
- The handout says LH "peaks" in the luteal phase; textbooks place the LH surge just before ovulation, with the corpus luteum then making progesterone.
- Confirm the exact day ranges for the phases; they vary by source.

## Related topics
[[Hormonal Control of the Menstrual Cycle]], [[Female Internal Genitalia: Vagina, Uterus and Decidua]]

title: Obstetric Terms: Zygote to Viability and Gravida-TPAL
body:
## Stages of prenatal development (age of gestation, AOG)
- **Zygote:** result of fertilization, up to about 2 weeks.
- **Embryo:** from implantation until organs form, about 2 to under 8 weeks.
- **Fetus:** 8 weeks to birth.
- **Implantation:** the growing structure attaches to the endometrium about 8-10 days after fertilization.

## Viability
The fetus can live outside the uterus: **24 weeks and above** per the handout (elsewhere it also mentions 500 g, see [[Spontaneous and Induced Abortion]]).

## Gravida and TPAL
- **Gravida:** number of pregnancies, counted regardless of outcome.
- **TPAL:** **T**erm births (38-42 weeks in the handout), **P**reterm births (under 37 weeks), **A**bortions, **L**iving children.
- **Nulligravid:** never pregnant.
- **Nullipara:** has never delivered a viable infant. The handout's wording mixes this up with gravidity.

## Worked example (made up)
A woman who is pregnant for the third time, with one earlier term baby and one earlier preterm baby (both alive), is G3 and T1 P1 A0 L2: the current pregnancy counts toward gravida but not yet toward para.

## How the exam asks about it
Computing G and TPAL from a short history, and telling embryo from fetus by weeks.

## Check against your textbook
- "Nulliparous" in the handout ("had been pregnant before but never given birth to a viable infant") is a muddled definition; check your local textbook.
- Term is usually 37-42 weeks; the handout says 38-42.

## Related topics
[[Signs of Pregnancy: Presumptive, Probable and Positive]], [[Post-term Pregnancy]]

title: Signs of Pregnancy: Presumptive, Probable and Positive
body:
## How the three groups differ
- **Presumptive:** subjective, felt by the woman; least reliable.
- **Probable:** can be documented by the examiner; still not proof.
- **Positive:** only the fetus itself can cause it; diagnostic.

## Presumptive signs
- Breast tenderness, fullness, darker areola.
- Nausea and vomiting (rising hCG). Relief: dry unsalted crackers, ice chips, small frequent low-fat meals, ambulation.
- Amenorrhea.
- Urinary frequency (uterus presses on the bladder, first and third trimesters).
- Fatigue (higher metabolic need).
- **Quickening:** mother feels fetal movement at about 18-20 weeks.
- Skin changes: melasma/chloasma (mask of pregnancy), linea nigra (pubis to navel), striae gravidarum (silvery stretch marks).

## Probable signs
- Positive pregnancy test (hCG), detectable about 10-14 days after the missed period; hCG peaks about 10 weeks.
- Abdominal enlargement, symmetrical and globular ([[Fundic Height Landmarks in Pregnancy]]).
- **Chadwick's:** bluish-purple vagina/cervix from more blood vessels.
- **Goodell's:** softened cervix.
- **Hegar's:** softened lower uterine segment.
- **Ballottement:** fetus rebounds when the lower uterus is tapped, about 16-20 weeks.
- **Braxton-Hicks:** periodic painless tightening, from about 28 weeks.

## Positive signs
- Fetal heart tones.
- Fetal movement felt by the examiner.
- Fetus seen on ultrasound or X-ray ([[Ultrasound in Pregnancy]]).

## How the exam asks about it
Classify a finding into presumptive/probable/positive. Nausea and quickening are presumptive; Chadwick's and a positive hCG test are probable; fetal heart tones are positive.

## Memory aid
Positive signs = "the baby itself shows up". Made up.

## Related topics
[[Obstetric Terms: Zygote to Viability and Gravida-TPAL]], [[Fundic Height Landmarks in Pregnancy]], [[Prenatal Visits, Blood Pressure and Leopold's Maneuvers]]

title: Fundic Height Landmarks in Pregnancy
body:
## What it is
Measuring from the top of the symphysis pubis to the top of the fundus with a tape (centimeters) is a quick way to estimate the age of gestation and spot growth problems.

## Landmarks from the handout
- **12 weeks:** fundus at the symphysis pubis.
- **16 weeks:** halfway between symphysis and umbilicus.
- **20 weeks:** at the umbilicus.
- Each additional centimeter above the umbilicus is about 4 more weeks: +1 cm = 24 weeks, +2 = 28, +3 = 32, +4 = 36 weeks (xiphoid level).
- **40 weeks:** about 1 cm below the xiphoid process (the baby drops/engages before labor).

## Nursing points
- The woman lies supine with legs flexed for abdominal assessment; use the centimeter side of the tape.
- A fundus much bigger than expected suggests multiple pregnancy ([[Multiple Pregnancy and Twin Types]]), hydramnios or a mole ([[Hydatidiform Mole]]); smaller than expected suggests poor fetal growth or oligohydramnios ([[Amniocentesis and Amniotic Fluid]]).

## How the exam asks about it
Estimate weeks of gestation from a fundal level, or decide what an unexpectedly large uterus might mean.

## Check against your textbook
The "+1 cm = 4 weeks" rule above the umbilicus is the handout's simplification; the common McDonald's rule is fundal height in cm approximately equals weeks of gestation after about 20 weeks.

## Related topics
[[Signs of Pregnancy: Presumptive, Probable and Positive]], [[Prenatal Visits, Blood Pressure and Leopold's Maneuvers]]

title: Prenatal Visits, Blood Pressure and Leopold's Maneuvers
body:
## Prenatal visit schedule
- Up to 28 weeks: every 4 weeks.
- 28-36 weeks: every 2 weeks.
- 36 weeks onward: every week.

## Taking blood pressure
Rest the mother about 15 minutes first. Position changes the reading: **sitting highest, supine in between, left lateral lowest**. Use the same position each visit for fair comparison.

## Abdominal assessment
Supine, legs flexed. Inspect for striae and linea nigra, then measure fundic height ([[Fundic Height Landmarks in Pregnancy]]).

## Leopold's maneuvers
Purpose: find fetal presentation and position.

Preparation, and why:
- Have her void first: a full bladder blocks palpation and is uncomfortable.
- Knees slightly flexed, small pillow or towel under one side: relaxes the abdomen and tilts the uterus off the vena cava, preventing supine hypotensive syndrome.
- Warm hands/water: comfort and no abdominal tightening.
- Face her head for maneuvers 1-3; face her feet for the fourth.

The four:
1. **Fundal:** what lies in the fundus; head (firm, round, moves separately) or breech (softer, moves with the body). Gives presentation.
2. **Lateral:** locates the fetal **back** (smooth, hard). Knobby parts are limbs. **Fetal heart tones are heard best over the back.**
3. **Pelvic (Pawlik):** what sits at the inlet and whether it is engaged. Not engaged = it moves up or sideways; engaged = firmly settled.
4. **Pelvic brim:** attitude and degree of extension; done only if the fetus is cephalic.

## How the exam asks about it
Where to place the stethoscope for fetal heart tones, why the mother voids first, and why a pillow is used under one side. Position terms are in [[Fetal Lie, Attitude, Presentation, Position and Station]].

## Related topics
[[Fundic Height Landmarks in Pregnancy]], [[Fetal Lie, Attitude, Presentation, Position and Station]], [[Body Changes in Pregnancy: Heart, Blood and Lungs]]

title: Body Changes in Pregnancy: Heart, Blood and Lungs
body:
## Cardiovascular
- Heart is pushed upward, left and forward.
- Cardiac output rises about 25-50%; heart rate rises about 10 bpm.
- Pressure from the uterus on veins slows circulation, causing edema and varicosities of legs, vulva and rectum.
- **Supine hypotensive syndrome:** the uterus presses on the vena cava when lying flat. **Position of choice: left lateral (Sims').**

## Blood
Plasma volume rises more than red cells, so blood is diluted: **physiologic anemia**. Teach iron-rich foods and supplements to meet higher iron needs.

## Respiratory
- Shortness of breath from uterine enlargement.
- Oxygen use up as much as 20% and breathing volume up to 40%.
- Tendency to over-breathe (hyperventilate), causing respiratory alkalosis: tingling in the extremities, light-headedness. Help: breathe slowly into a paper bag or cupped hands.

## Priority nursing action
For dizziness or a low BP when supine, turn her to her left side first (restores venous return; Maslow: circulation before teaching).

## How the exam asks about it
Why physiologic anemia is "normal" yet iron is still given, and the best position for a pregnant woman. Heart disease implications are in [[Heart Disease in Pregnancy]].

## Related topics
[[Body Changes in Pregnancy: Digestive, Kidney, Thyroid and Back]], [[Heart Disease in Pregnancy]]

title: Body Changes in Pregnancy: Digestive, Kidney, Thyroid and Back
body:
## Digestive discomforts
- **Pica:** craving non-food substances (clay, chalk, dirt, starch). Counsel on risks and check for anemia.
- **Epulis:** gum swelling that bleeds easily (estrogen). Use a soft toothbrush, avoid strong mouthwash.
- **Ptyalism:** excess saliva. Hard candies can help.
- **Heartburn:** the uterus crowds the stomach and slows emptying. Do not lie down after eating, walk gently, eat small frequent meals.

## Kidney and bladder
Hormones relax the ureters and renal pelvis and the growing uterus compresses the bladder: urinary **frequency** and urine stasis, so higher **UTI risk**.

## Thyroid
The handout warns that hyperthyroidism is a pregnancy risk and thyroid storm (arrhythmias, possible death) is dangerous in labor. Watch for its signs.

## Muscles and bones
- **Relaxin** loosens pelvic joints.
- **Diastasis recti:** rectus muscles separate; normal and recovers after birth.
- **Physiologic lordosis** ("pride of pregnancy") and back pain: pelvic rocking, direct pressure on the lumbar area, avoid lying flat; the handout says no analgesics.

## How the exam asks about it
Match a discomfort with the best self-care measure. Safe, non-drug measures first (assess, teach, then medicate).

## Check against your textbook
- The handout says pica may come from hypersalivation; the usual teaching links it to nutrient deficiency or cultural factors.
- "No analgesic" for back pain should be checked with your textbook and prescriber guidance.
- "Greatest risk for hyperthyroidism" is worded loosely.

## Related topics
[[Body Changes in Pregnancy: Heart, Blood and Lungs]], [[Postpartum Infection and Endometritis]]
