title: Obstetric Numbers and Cut-offs Review
body:
## What it is
All the figures from the handout, grouped so they can be rehearsed quickly. Memorize the handout numbers; do not substitute figures from other sources without checking.

## Cycle and early pregnancy
- Cycle 28 days (range 23-35). Flow 4-6 days normal; blood loss 30-80 mL.
- Proliferative phase 6-14 days, variable. Luteal phase constant 14 days. Corpus luteum regresses after 8-10 days if no fertilization.
- Implantation 8-10 days after fertilization. Zygote under 2 weeks; embryo 2 to under 8 weeks; fetus 8 weeks to birth. Viability 24 weeks and above.
- Quickening 18-20 weeks. Ballottement 16-20 weeks. Braxton-Hicks from 28 weeks.
- hCG detectable 10-14 days after missed period; peak about 10 weeks.

## Fundal height
12 weeks symphysis; 16 weeks halfway to umbilicus; 20 weeks umbilicus; 24 weeks +1 cm; 28 weeks +2 cm; 32 weeks +3 cm; 36 weeks +4 cm (xiphoid); 40 weeks 1 cm below xiphoid.

## Visits
Every 4 weeks up to 28 weeks; every 2 weeks 28-36 weeks; weekly from 36 weeks.

## Tests
- Amniotic fluid normal 800-1200 mL; oligohydramnios under 500; hydramnios over 1200. L:S ratio 2:1 mature.
- Amniocentesis at 14-16 weeks; observe 30 minutes after. Chorionic villi sampling 8-10 weeks. AFP peak 13th-32nd week.
- Biophysical score 8-10 normal, 6 suspicious, 4 in jeopardy. Reactive NST: 2 accelerations of 15 beats for 15 seconds in 20 minutes. CST best around 38 weeks.
- Oral glucose: 50 g at 24-28 weeks; above 140 at 1 hour leads to the 3-hour 100 g test; fasting above 95.

## Labor
- Latent phase 0-3 cm; active 4-7 cm; transition 8-10 cm. Contractions: latent 20-40 s every 5-10 min; active 40-60 s every 3-5 min; transition 60-90 s every 2-3 min.
- Second stage: first-time mother 1-4 hours; multigravida 20-45 minutes.
- Third stage 5-10 minutes; abnormal beyond 30 minutes. Cotyledons 16-20.
- Fourth stage first 1-4 hours.
- Precipitate labor under 3 hours.

## Complications and postpartum
- Pre-eclampsia 140/90 (mild); severe 160/110. Proteinuria over 250 mg/dL in the module; severe: more than 5 g/24 h.
- Post-term beyond 42 weeks. Preterm before 37 weeks (module says before end of week 37).
- Puerperium 6 weeks; involution about 1 cm a day. Lochia rubra 1-3, serosa 3-10, alba 10 onward to 3-6 weeks.
- Cesarean birth rate should not exceed 20% of deliveries (module).

## How the exam asks about it
Straight recall or "which is abnormal". The trap is mixing similar numbers (14 days luteal vs 14-16 weeks amniocentesis).

## Related topics
[[Fundic Height Landmarks in Pregnancy]], [[Biophysical Profile and Non-Stress Test]], [[First Stage of Labor and Nitrazine Test]], [[Pregnancy-Induced Hypertension: Classification and Pre-eclampsia]], [[Lochia and Return of Menstruation]]

## Check against your textbook
The module itself gives preterm as both under 37 weeks and "before the end of week 37", and TPAL term as 38-42 weeks while post-term is beyond 42; confirm which cut-offs your exam uses. Handout blood loss and diastolic criteria are older standards.

title: Responding to Non-Reassuring Fetal Status: Cause, Pattern and Action
body:
## What it is
A cause-to-action map for fetal distress in labor. The exam gives a tracing or a situation and asks for the first nursing action.

## Must-know facts
- Late deceleration: uteroplacental insufficiency. Variable: cord compression. Early: head compression (benign).
- Oxytocin causes strong contractions that reduce placental blood flow, so it is the first thing to stop when late decelerations appear.
- Supine position presses the uterus on the vena cava and lowers blood return; side-lying corrects it.

## Priority nursing actions (in order, with the reason)
1. **Late decelerations:** stop or slow oxytocin; turn the woman to the left side; give IV fluids; give oxygen (the module's CST note states 8-10 liters per minute by mask); watch the strip. If decelerations continue or the baseline is lost, prepare for prompt delivery (cesarean). Why: restore oxygen supply to the placenta first.
2. **Variable decelerations:** change position (side-lying or Trendelenburg) to take weight off the cord; the physician may order amnioinfusion.
3. **Cord prolapse:** do not push the cord back; cover it with gauze moistened with normal saline; give oxygen; relieve pressure on the cord by position; check fetal heart tones; prepare for immediate delivery. Why: the cord is the baby's oxygen line.
4. **Ruptured membranes:** note the time; infection risk climbs after 24 hours; check fetal heart tones at once because of cord prolapse risk.
5. **Bleeding with fetal distress** (abruptio): lateral position, oxygen, fluids, outright delivery if distress is present.

## Complications and red flags
Persistent late decelerations, absent variability, bradycardia, thick meconium (except in breech), maternal fever, cord visible at the vagina.

## How to reason about it
Cause -> pattern -> action: the action removes the cause (oxytocin off, pressure off the cord, vena cava free). The trap: giving more oxytocin to "speed things up" or calling the physician before stopping the oxytocin; start the simple safe action, then notify.

## Related topics
[[Fetal Heart Rate Patterns and Decelerations]], [[Preterm Rupture of Membranes and Cord Prolapse]], [[Contraction Stress Test and Late Deceleration Response]], [[Abruptio Placentae]], [[Breech Presentation Types]]

## Check against your textbook
The module lists "outright delivery" as a possible step but timing and method are physician decisions. Amnioinfusion is named only briefly; confirm the indications.

title: Common Discomforts of Pregnancy and Nursing Relief
body:
## What it is
Common, expected body complaints in pregnancy with the safe nursing measure for each. Most are physiologic, so the exam wants the simple teaching answer.

## Must-know facts and relief
- **Nausea and vomiting** (hCG rise, early pregnancy): dry unsalted crackers, ice chips, small frequent meals, less fatty food, gentle ambulation.
- **Frequent urination:** first and third trimesters; the growing uterus presses on the bladder. Reassure; urinary stasis from relaxed ureters also raises UTI risk, so report burning.
- **Heartburn:** the uterus pushes the stomach upward and the gut slows. Do not lie flat after eating; walk gradually; eat small frequent meals.
- **Pica:** craving non-food items (clay, chalk, dirt, soil, metal, pencils). Do not criticise; assess, check for anemia, offer safer choices.
- **Epulis (gum swelling and bleeding):** estrogen. Soft toothbrush, avoid strong mouthwash.
- **Ptyalism (too much saliva):** offer hard candies.
- **Hyperventilation and respiratory alkalosis:** tingling in the extremities, light-headedness. Breathe slowly into a paper bag or cupped hands.
- **Supine hypotension syndrome:** dizziness and low blood pressure lying on the back; turn to left lateral position.
- **Back pain and physiologic lordosis ("pride of pregnancy"):** pelvic rocking, firm pressure on the lower back, avoid lying flat; the handout says avoid analgesics.
- **Leg swelling and varicosities:** slowed circulation; avoid prolonged standing, elevate legs, use left side lying.
- **Physiologic anemia:** blood dilution; take iron and iron-rich foods.
- **Diastasis recti:** separation of the abdominal muscle; normal and reverses after birth.

## Red flags (not routine)
Vomiting that prevents eating, severe headache, vision change, sudden swelling of face and hands (think pre-eclampsia), persistent dizziness, painful urination, vaginal bleeding.

## How to reason about it
Physiologic -> reassure and teach a simple measure. The trap: treating a normal complaint with medication, or missing a red flag that is a warning of a complication.

## How the exam asks about it
"Which instruction should the nurse give a woman with ..." Choose the non-drug measure.

## Related topics
[[Body Changes in Pregnancy: Digestive, Kidney, Thyroid and Back]], [[Body Changes in Pregnancy: Heart, Blood and Lungs]], [[Signs of Pregnancy: Presumptive, Probable and Positive]], [[Pregnancy-Induced Hypertension: Classification and Pre-eclampsia]]

## Check against your textbook
"No analgesic" for back pain and the claim that pica comes from excess saliva are the handout's statements; confirm. Safety of any remedy should be checked with the prenatal care provider.

title: Lactational Amenorrhea and Return of Fertility After Birth
body:
## What it is
The module teaches that breastfeeding can delay menstruation and ovulation, and lists when periods and intercourse usually resume. It is a natural method, not a guarantee.

## Must-know facts
- **Three requirements for lactational amenorrhea:** (1) the mother breastfeeds exclusively; (2) she has no menstruation (some suppression of ovulation); (3) it is within 6 months postpartum.
- If the mother is **not breastfeeding**, menstruation returns about **6-10 weeks** after birth.
- If she **is breastfeeding**, menstruation may take about **6 months** to return.
- Intercourse is generally allowed after **3-4 weeks** (once bleeding settles and the perineum heals).
- Ovulation can happen before the first period, so a woman can become pregnant before menses return.

## Priority nursing actions
Teach all three conditions together; ask about exclusive feeding, whether periods have returned and the baby's age; recommend another method (see [[Reproductive Health and Family Planning]]) when any condition changes. Why: the method fails as soon as one requirement is no longer met.

## Client teaching
- Feed on demand, day and night, with no formula or regular supplements.
- Once periods return, or at 6 months, or when feeding reduces, add another method.
- Sexual activity: wait until bleeding has eased and any episiotomy has healed; use a water-based lubricant if dry.

## How the exam asks about it
"Which statement shows understanding of the lactational amenorrhea method?" The correct answer includes all three conditions.

## How to reason about it
The trap is the answer that says breastfeeding always prevents pregnancy.

## Related topics
[[Lochia and Return of Menstruation]], [[Puerperium: Involution and Rubin's Phases]], [[Family Planning Methods: Permanent, Hormonal and Barrier]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout states 6-10 weeks and 6 months as typical returns; real timing varies. Details such as lubricant advice are general knowledge added here.

title: Postpartum Psychosis and Emotional Problems After Birth
body:
## What it is
The module places postpartum psychosis in the taking-hold phase and calls it a brief psychotic episode lasting up to about 3 months. It is a mental-health emergency, different from the common "baby blues".

## Must-know facts
- Psychosis involves loss of contact with reality: delusions, hallucinations, confusion, severe agitation or withdrawal.
- It is far more serious than mild tearfulness, which is expected in the early days.
- The mother can be a danger to herself or the baby, so safety is the top concern.

## Assessment
Sleeplessness, strange or suspicious talk, not recognising or rejecting the baby, severe mood swings, thoughts of harming self or baby.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Keep mother and baby safe; do not leave the baby alone with a mother who is psychotic or having harmful thoughts. Why: safety is the second level of Maslow, right after survival needs.
2. Stay calm, speak simply, do not argue with delusions.
3. Report to the physician immediately for evaluation and treatment.
4. Maintain a quiet environment and observe closely.

## Client and family teaching
Warning signs to report, the need for follow-up, and that this is an illness, not a failing as a parent.

## How the exam asks about it
A new mother says she hears voices telling her about the baby: the answer is to ensure safety and notify the doctor, not reassurance alone.

## Related topics
[[Puerperium: Involution and Rubin's Phases]], [[Fourth Stage of Labor and Postpartum Checks]], [[Mood Disorder Theories and Variants]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout is a one-line mention. Timing (usually the first weeks), the difference between blues, depression and psychosis, and the treatment details are not in the handout.

title: Cesarean Birth, Trial of Labor and Factors That Block Normal Birth
body:
## What it is
A collection of the situations in the module where normal vaginal birth may be difficult or unsafe, and what the module says about cesarean birth.

## Must-know facts
- **Cephalopelvic disproportion (CPD):** the fetal head is larger than the maternal pelvis. Even with CPD, a **trial of labor** is usually allowed first; cesarean is not automatic. Cesarean births should not exceed about 20% of all deliveries.
- **Fetal lie:** a transverse lie means dilation will not progress.
- **Fetal attitude:** complete extension (face presentation) prevents progress; the face cannot normally enter the pelvis.
- **Pelvic type:** android (narrow outlet) and platypelloid (shallow inlet) make labor harder; gynecoid is ideal.
- **Shirodkar cerclage:** delivery is by cesarean.
- **Placenta previa:** total previa blocks the cervix.
- **Abruptio placentae:** outright delivery for fetal distress; hysterectomy for atony.
- **Cord prolapse, persistent late decelerations, premature rupture with infection:** prompt delivery.
- **Prolonged rupture of membranes over 24 hours without birth:** infection risk, and the module states cesarean may be needed.
- **Breech:** cord prolapse and head entrapment risk.
- **Positive contraction stress test lasting over 10 minutes:** cesarean may be needed.

## Priority nursing actions
Prepare the woman and family (consent, explanation), keep NPO as ordered, start IV, check fetal heart rate, and give postoperative care: assess fundus, lochia (cesarean women also have lochia), pain, bladder, bowel, wound and breathing. Why: airway and circulation, then comfort and bonding.

## How to reason about it
Cause -> finding -> priority action: obstructed labor or fetal distress -> cesarean preparation. The trap: "CPD means automatic cesarean"; the module says a trial of labor comes first.

## Related topics
[[Pelvis Types, Cephalopelvic Disproportion and Fetal Diameters]], [[Fetal Lie, Attitude, Presentation, Position and Station]], [[Placenta Previa]], [[Breech Presentation Types]], [[Responding to Non-Reassuring Fetal Status: Cause, Pattern and Action]]

## Check against your textbook
The 20% figure and the cesarean-after-24-hours rule are the handout's statements; many authorities no longer rely on a fixed cesarean rate or on 24 hours alone.
